title: LLM fundamentals
description: How language models read, generate, retrieve, learn, cost, and go wrong.

cards.question: Why do LLMs often miscount the letters in a word?
options: Their vocabulary has no single letters
They see tokens, not individual characters
cards.explanation: Text is split into tokens that often span several characters, so the model never directly sees each letter it is asked to count.

cards.question: A model's context window limits prompt and generated tokens combined.
cards.explanation: Input and output share one window, so a very long prompt leaves less room for the reply.

cards.question: What does a tokenizer do?
options: Compresses the prompt to save bandwidth
Encrypts text before it reaches the model
Maps text to IDs from a fixed vocabulary
cards.explanation: A tokenizer splits text into pieces from a fixed vocabulary and maps each to an integer ID. The model reads and writes these IDs.

cards.question: The model itself keeps no memory between requests; earlier turns must be in the context.
cards.explanation: Model weights do not change per request. Chat apps resend (or server-side store and replay) prior turns so the model can see them.

cards.question: Research on long prompts found models most often overlook facts placed where?
options: In the middle of the context
cards.explanation: The 'lost in the middle' study found recall is best near the start and end of a long context and worst in the middle.

cards.question: What does lowering the sampling temperature do?
options: Makes output more focused and predictable
Lets the model use more context
cards.explanation: Lower temperature sharpens the probability distribution so likely tokens win more often. Higher temperature flattens it for more variety.

cards.question: Setting temperature to 0 guarantees identical output on every API call.
cards.explanation: Temperature 0 is near-greedy, but batching, floating-point effects and infrastructure changes can still make outputs differ between calls.

cards.question: What does top-p (nucleus) sampling do?
options: Always picks the p most likely tokens
Samples from top tokens summing to probability p
cards.explanation: Top-p keeps the smallest set of most likely tokens whose probabilities add up to p, then samples only from that set.

cards.question: At each step, what does the model produce before a token is chosen?
options: A probability for every token in its vocabulary
An embedding of the whole answer
cards.explanation: The model outputs scores over its whole vocabulary. A sampling strategy such as greedy, temperature or top-p then picks one token.

cards.question: Greedy decoding always picks the single most likely next token.
cards.explanation: Greedy decoding takes the highest-probability token at each step. It is deterministic in principle but can get repetitive.

cards.question: What is a text embedding?
options: A compressed copy of the text
A list of the text's keywords
A vector that captures the text's meaning
cards.explanation: An embedding model maps text to a vector of numbers so that texts with similar meaning land close together.

cards.question: Which measure is most commonly used to compare two text embeddings?
cards.explanation: Cosine similarity compares the angle between two vectors, a standard way to judge how close two embeddings are in meaning.

cards.question: RAG retrieves relevant documents at query time and adds them to the prompt.
cards.explanation: Retrieval-augmented generation searches a knowledge source for each query and places the results in context so answers can cite them.

cards.question: Why split documents into chunks before embedding them for RAG?
options: Embedding models reject any file over 1 KB
Chunks turn vectors into exact keyword matches
Retrieved pieces stay focused and fit in context
Chunking removes the need for a vector index
cards.explanation: One vector for a whole long document blurs its meaning. Smaller chunks match queries more precisely and use less of the context window.

cards.question: Updating what a RAG system knows requires retraining the model.
cards.explanation: You update the document store and its index. The model reads fresh content at query time, which is a key advantage of RAG.

cards.question: What task is a base model mainly trained on during pretraining?
cards.explanation: Pretraining teaches a model to predict the next token over huge amounts of text. Instruction tuning and preference training come later.

cards.question: Fine-tuning changes a model's weights; prompting does not.
cards.explanation: Fine-tuning continues training on new examples and updates weights. A prompt only changes the input for one request.

cards.question: In RLHF, what does the reward model learn from?
cards.explanation: People rank or compare responses. A reward model learns those preferences, and reinforcement learning tunes the LLM to score well on it.

cards.question: During inference, a model learns from your conversation and keeps that knowledge for others.
cards.explanation: Inference does not update weights. Anything the model 'learns' in a chat lives only in that context unless a later training run includes it.

cards.question: Why might a model not know a library released last month?
options: Libraries are filtered from training data
Its training data has a cutoff date
Its tokenizer lacks the library's name
cards.explanation: A model only knows what was in its training data, which ends at a cutoff. Give it current docs in context to fill the gap.

cards.question: What does prompt caching reuse between requests?
options: Model weights stored on your device
Processing of a repeated prompt prefix
cards.explanation: The provider stores the computed state for an identical prompt prefix, so later requests that share it are faster and cheaper to process.

cards.question: Prompt caching works best when stable content like instructions comes first in the prompt.
cards.explanation: Caches match on an exact prefix. Put unchanging parts first and the varying parts last so the shared prefix stays as long as possible.

cards.question: For a long response, what usually dominates total latency?
options: Generating output tokens one at a time
cards.explanation: Output is produced token by token, each step depending on the last. Long outputs take time roughly in proportion to their length.

cards.question: Hosted LLM APIs typically charge more per output token than per input token.
cards.explanation: Output tokens are generated one at a time and cost more compute each, so most providers price them several times higher than input.

cards.question: What does streaming a model's response mainly improve?
options: Time until the first words appear
cards.explanation: Streaming sends tokens as they are generated. Total work is the same, but users see output almost immediately.

cards.question: What is an LLM hallucination?
options: Fluent output that is false or unsupported
A response cut off by the token limit
cards.explanation: Models generate plausible text, not verified facts. A hallucination reads confidently but invents APIs, citations or details.

cards.question: A confident tone in a model's answer is a reliable sign that it is correct.
cards.explanation: Models sound equally fluent when right and wrong. Verify claims with tests, docs or sources rather than trusting tone.

cards.question: What most reduces hallucinations about your own codebase?
options: Asking the model to be confident
Giving the model the relevant files
cards.explanation: Grounding the model in the actual source lets it read real names and signatures instead of guessing from training data.

cards.question: What does 'LLM-as-a-judge' mean?
options: A model that writes legal text
Using a model to grade model outputs
cards.explanation: A model scores outputs against a rubric. It scales well for fuzzy criteria, but should be checked against human judgments.

cards.question: Scoring a prompt only on the examples you tuned it with can overstate its quality.
cards.explanation: Like overfitting in ML, a prompt tweaked to pass specific cases may fail on new ones. Keep a held-out set for honest measurement.
